raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the survival benefit of ICD therapy while avoiding transvenous and intracardiac hardware. In the S-ICD, the generator is positioned in the left lateral thoracic region and a parasternal electrode senses and defibrillates without entering the venous system or heart. Early feasibility work showed reliable induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmia conversion [1], and the START study supported the concept that surface/subcutaneous morphology algorithms could discriminate supraventricular from ventricular tachyarrhythmias [2]. The pivotal IDE study then demonstrated high acute conversion efficacy and acceptable early safety in patients with ICD indications but no need for pacing [3].

The clinical niche of the S-ICD is best understood by contrasting what it avoids and what it cannot provide. By eliminating endovascular leads, it reduces exposure to lead fracture, venous occlusion, tricuspid valve interaction, cardiac perforation, and systemic lead infection. However, because it has no intracardiac electrode, it cannot deliver chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or painless antitachycardia pacing (ATP). Thus, ideal candidates are patients requiring defibrillation only: younger patients with long lifetime lead-risk exposure, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, limited venous access, prior device infection, or dialysis-dependent kidney failure, provided that monomorphic VT likely to respond to ATP and future pacing needs are unlikely [28], [29].

Prospective registries established the S-ICD as a durable therapy. Early EFFORTLESS registry data and pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS analyses confirmed high shock efficacy, absence of endocarditis, and complication rates that improved with operator experience [4], [5]. Midterm and long-term EFFORTLESS follow-up showed sustained arrhythmia termination, relatively infrequent conversion to transvenous systems for pacing indications, and the importance of continued surveillance for infection, erosion, inappropriate shock, and generator replacement issues [6], [7]. The UNTOUCHED trial extended these observations to a more conventional primary-prevention, low-ejection-fraction population using contemporary programming, showing a low 18-month inappropriate shock rate despite substantial comorbidity [8]. The large US post-approval study confirmed high 5-year shock efficacy and low electrode-related complication rates in real-world practice [12], [13].

Randomized comparative evidence is now central to decision-making. PRAETORIAN showed that S-ICD therapy was noninferior to transvenous ICD therapy for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks in patients without pacing indications [9]. Subsequent analyses clarified trade-offs: appropriate shock efficacy was similar, but transvenous ICDs provided ATP for some ventricular tachycardia episodes, whereas S-ICDs avoided most lead-related complications [10], [11]. Observational comparisons and meta-analyses broadly support comparable mortality and overall major outcomes, with lower lead-related complications for S-ICD and a different profile of pocket complications and inappropriate shocks [14], [15], [30].

Implant technique has evolved substantially. The original three-incision subcutaneous approach has largely been replaced by two-incision techniques and intermuscular generator placement, which improve cosmesis, stability, and defibrillation vectors [17]. Preimplant ECG screening is mandatory because sensing depends on a favorable QRS/T-wave relationship in at least one vector and posture; failure is more common with wide QRS complexes, hypertrophy, cardiomyopathy, and certain channelopathies [20], [21]. T-wave oversensing remains the signature mechanism of inappropriate S-ICD shock, although contemporary filtering, dual-zone programming, exercise template optimization, and careful vector selection have reduced its incidence [22], [23]. The PRAETORIAN score uses postimplant radiographs to quantify generator and coil position and intervening fat, providing an anatomic correlate of defibrillation success [18]. Recent randomized PRAETORIAN-DFT data suggest that in optimally positioned systems, omission of defibrillation testing may be safe, although practice should remain individualized until guidelines incorporate these findings [19].

Special populations illustrate both the appeal and limitations of the S-ICD. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the absence of transvenous leads is attractive for young patients, but hypertrophy and dynamic repolarization can increase screening failure or oversensing risk [24], [25]. Pediatric and congenital heart disease cohorts show feasibility when anatomy or venous access makes transvenous systems undesirable, but body size, growth, complex QRS morphology, and need for future pacing require careful selection [26], [27]. In Brugada syndrome, S-ICD therapy avoids lead complications in generally young patients, yet high right-precordial ST/T-wave variability and fever- or drug-induced ECG changes can challenge sensing [29].

In summary, the S-ICD is no longer a niche device but a mature alternative to the transvenous ICD for patients who need defibrillation without pacing. Its value is greatest when lifetime lead preservation, infection avoidance, or venous access are priorities. Contemporary implantation technique, programming, screening, and imaging have improved safety, but patient selection remains decisive: the central question is not whether the S-ICD works, but whether a given patient will need pacing or ATP during the life of the system [16].
